note: Keep, the third tab: words by heart, things every Christian once knew, faith at home, and a rule of life. Draft: every claim is listed in content/review/keep-notes.json for a reviewer. Scripture is the World English Bible; other set texts follow the Learn rule (public domain).

intro.title: Make it yours
intro.line: What you carry in your head and keep in your home. The words people have known by heart for centuries, the things every Christian once knew, and the small rituals that turn a house into a place of faith.

why: For most of history, the educated carried their learning in their heads. Many monks knew all hundred and fifty psalms by heart; schoolchildren recited Virgil and the catechism; preachers, poets and statesmen quoted Scripture and Shakespeare without looking anything up.

What you know by heart you can think with, pray with and lean on when there is nothing else: on a sleepless night, in a hospital corridor, at a graveside. You don't really own a text you have to look up.
byheart.how: Climb the ladder from the first rung. Each piece has four steps: read it aloud, fill the gaps, first letters only, then say it from memory. Come back after a few days, then a week, then a month, and it will stay.

rungs.title: First words
rungs.line: The words Christians everywhere have always known. Start here.

rungs.title: The Psalms
rungs.line: The Church's first prayer book: words for joy, fear, guilt, age and hope.

rungs.title: Scripture to live by
rungs.line: The verses people have built their lives on, from Genesis to Paul.

rungs.title: Songs and creeds of the Church
rungs.line: What the Church has sung and said together for centuries.

rungs.title: Athens and Rome
rungs.line: The classics a Christian education always carried: Homer, Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Virgil and the Stoics.

rungs.title: The great Christian writers and poets
rungs.line: Augustine, Dante and Julian; Shakespeare, Donne, Herbert, Milton and Hopkins.

people.title: They knew it by heart
people.line: For most of history, educated people carried great words in their heads. It was not a party trick. It was what they had to think with, and what held them up when everything else was taken away.

items.name: Jesus
items.what: answered every temptation in the desert with words of Scripture he knew by heart, and died praying a psalm (Matthew 4; Psalm 22; Mark 15:34).

items.name: The monks of St Benedict
items.what: sang all 150 psalms every week under Benedict's Rule (about 530). Many knew the whole psalter by heart.

items.name: Augustine
items.what: learned Virgil by heart as a schoolboy, and admits he wept over Dido before he ever wept over his own soul (Confessions I.13).

items.name: Abraham Lincoln
items.what: had only a year or so of schooling, but knew long passages of the King James Bible and Shakespeare by heart. His great speeches are full of both.

items.name: Frederick Douglass
items.what: taught himself to read as a slave and learned the speeches in The Columbian Orator by heart. He became the greatest orator of his age.

items.name: Winston Churchill
items.what: won a prize at Harrow for reciting twelve hundred lines of Macaulay's Lays of Ancient Rome without a mistake (My Early Life, 1930), and could recite poetry for hours all his life.

items.name: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
items.what: prayed the psalms and the hymns of Paul Gerhardt that he knew by heart in a Nazi prison cell, before his execution in 1945.

items.name: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn
items.what: composed thousands of lines of verse in the Soviet labour camps and kept them in his memory, counting them on a rosary made of bread (The Gulag Archipelago).

items.name: Nelson Mandela
items.what: and his fellow prisoners on Robben Island kept Henley's poem 'Invictus' in their heads; he recited it to the men around him.

know.line: Short lists that every Christian, and most of the West, once knew by heart. Each takes a minute to read and a week to learn.

items.title: The Ten Commandments
items.line: The ten words given at Sinai, the root of Western law.
list: You shall have no other gods before me.
You shall not make idols to worship.
You shall not misuse the name of the Lord your God.
Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.
Honour your father and your mother.
You shall not give false testimony against your neighbour.
You shall not covet anything that belongs to your neighbour.
items.note: Here in short form, as children have long learned them. Traditions number them differently: Catholics and Lutherans join the first two and divide the last; Jewish tradition counts 'I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of Egypt' as the first word.

items.title: The Great Commandment and the Golden Rule
items.line: Jesus's summary of the whole law.
list: Love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, mind and strength.
Whatever you desire for men to do to you, you shall also do to them (Matthew 7:12).
items.note: The first two are Jesus quoting the Law of Moses (Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18). The Golden Rule has negative forms in many cultures, as in Hillel's 'What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour'; Jesus puts it positively.

items.title: The books of the Bible
items.line: Sixty-six books in two Testaments, in order.

groups.list: Joshua, Judges, Ruth, 1 and 2 Samuel, 1 and 2 Kings, 1 and 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther
Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs
Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi
Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 and 2 Thessalonians, 1 and 2 Timothy, Titus, Philemon
Hebrews, James, 1 and 2 Peter, 1, 2 and 3 John, Jude; Revelation

items.note: This is the Protestant order of 39 and 27 books. Catholic Bibles add seven more books to the Old Testament (Tobit, Judith, 1 and 2 Maccabees, Wisdom, Sirach and Baruch) and longer Esther and Daniel; Orthodox Bibles include a few more again. Jewish Bibles have the same books as the Protestant Old Testament, in a different order.

items.title: The twelve apostles
items.line: The twelve Jesus chose, a new Israel of twelve tribes.
items.note: Luke lists 'Judas the son of James' where Matthew and Mark have Thaddaeus; most take them to be the same man. After Judas Iscariot's death the apostles chose Matthias in his place (Acts 1:26).

items.title: The Christian year
items.line: The year told as the story of Christ, season by season.
list: Advent: four Sundays of waiting before Christmas (purple or blue).
Christmas: twelve days, from 25 December (white or gold).
Epiphany, 6 January: the wise men; Christ shown to the nations.
Lent: forty days of fasting before Easter, from Ash Wednesday, not counting Sundays (purple).
Holy Week: Palm Sunday, Maundy Thursday, Good Friday, Holy Saturday.
Easter: fifty days of joy, from Easter Sunday (white or gold).
Ascension: the fortieth day of Easter.
Pentecost: the fiftieth day, the gift of the Spirit (red).
Ordinary Time: the long green seasons between, when the Church grows (green).
All Saints, 1 November: all the faithful, known and unknown.
items.note: The Orthodox keep the same pattern, mostly by the older Julian calendar, so their Easter usually falls later. Colours vary by church.

items.title: The seven virtues
items.line: Four from Athens, three from Paul: the shape of a good character.
list: Prudence: practical wisdom, seeing what to do.
Fortitude: courage in danger and endurance in pain.
Love: willing the good of another, for God's sake. 'The greatest of these is love.'
items.note: The first four, from Plato and the Stoics, were called 'cardinal' (from Latin cardo, a hinge) because every other virtue hinges on them. The last three, from Paul, are called 'theological' because they are directed to God.

items.title: The seven deadly sins
items.line: The old map of what quietly deforms us.
list: Sloth (acedia: a listless indifference to what matters)
items.note: The list grew from the desert monk Evagrius's eight 'evil thoughts' (fourth century) and took this form with Pope Gregory the Great (about 590). Dante's Purgatorio is built on it. 'Deadly' means they give birth to other sins, not that they are worse than murder.

items.title: The fruit of the Spirit
items.line: What a life looks like when God is at work in it.
items.note: Paul says 'fruit', not 'fruits': one harvest with nine flavours. They grow; they are not achieved by effort alone.

items.title: The works of mercy
items.line: What love does with its hands, and with its words.

groups.list: Feed the hungry. Give drink to the thirsty. Welcome the stranger. Clothe the naked. Visit the sick. Visit prisoners. Bury the dead.
Teach those who don't know. Counsel the doubtful. Correct those who go wrong. Bear wrongs patiently. Forgive offences. Comfort the sorrowful. Pray for the living and the dead.

items.note: The first six come from Jesus's parable of the sheep and the goats (Matthew 25); burying the dead comes from the book of Tobit. The lists were fixed in the Middle Ages and are kept especially by Catholics, but the practice belongs to every church.

items.title: The first questions
items.ref: Westminster Shorter Catechism (1647); Heidelberg Catechism (1563); Baltimore Catechism (1885)
items.line: How children were taught the heart of the faith, in a question and an answer.
list: What is the chief end of man? Man's chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever. (Westminster, Presbyterian)
What is your only comfort in life and in death? That I am not my own, but belong, body and soul, to my faithful Saviour Jesus Christ. (Heidelberg, Reformed; in our own words)
Why did God make you? God made me to know Him, to love Him, and to serve Him in this world, and to be happy with Him for ever in the next. (Baltimore, Catholic)
items.note: Three traditions, one answer: we are made for God, and for joy.

home.line: Faith is learned at the table and the bedside before it is learned anywhere else. Small, repeated things, done together. For families, couples and anyone living alone.

week.title: A day of rest
how: Stop one ordinary kind of work or shopping for the day.
Eat one slow meal together, with a candle.
Do one thing purely for joy: a walk, a game, music, a visit.
week.why: The Sabbath was the first law in history to give slaves, foreigners and animals a day off (Exodus 20:8–11). Christians moved their day to Sunday, the day of the resurrection.

week.title: A verse for the week
how: Read this week's piece at breakfast every day.
By Friday, try it with only the first letters.
On Sunday, see who can say it all.
week.why: Families learned Scripture this way for centuries, and children often outpace the adults.

week.title: One kindness together
week.line: Do one good thing as a household.
how: Choose it on Sunday: a meal for a neighbour, a card, a visit, a tidy-up for someone.
Do it together during the week.
Talk about it at dinner afterwards.
week.why: Children learn what love is by doing it alongside you, not by being told.

week.title: The giving jar
how: Keep a jar on the table.
Everyone puts something in each week, children too.
Decide together where it goes each month.
week.why: Jesus talked about money more than almost anything else. Giving loosens its grip.

week.title: An open table
how: Once a month, invite someone who might eat alone.
Keep it simple: soup is enough.
Say grace, and ask tonight's dinner question.
week.why: Hospitality to strangers was one of the marks of the first Christians (Romans 12:13; Hebrews 13:2).

year.title: The Advent wreath
how: Make a ring of greenery with four candles, and a white one in the middle if you like.
Each Sunday light one more candle, with a short reading and a prayer.
Light the white candle on Christmas Day.
year.why: The wreath began in Hamburg in 1839, when Johann Hinrich Wichern, who ran a home for poor boys, set candles on a cartwheel so the children could count the days to Christmas. Light growing in the dark is Advent's whole message.

year.title: Christmas Eve
how: Set out a nativity scene, and add the baby last.
Read Luke 2:1–20 aloud by candlelight.
Go to a midnight or carol service, or sing one carol at home.
year.why: Francis of Assisi made the first living nativity scene at Greccio in 1223, so people could see how poor the birth was.

year.title: Blessing the door at Epiphany
how: Read Matthew 2:1–12, the wise men.
With chalk, write the year and C+M+B above the front door, for example 20+C+M+B+27.
Pray that all who enter will be welcome, as Christ is.
year.why: C, M and B stand for the traditional names of the wise men, Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar, and for Christus mansionem benedicat, 'May Christ bless this house'. It is a Catholic and Lutheran custom, especially in central Europe.

year.title: Pancakes, then Lent
how: Make pancakes on Tuesday to use up the eggs and butter.
On Wednesday choose: one thing to give up, one thing to take on, one thing to give.
If you can, go to an Ash Wednesday service.
year.why: To be 'shriven' was to confess and be forgiven before Lent began. Ashes on Ash Wednesday recall God's words to Adam: 'you are dust, and you shall return to dust' (Genesis 3:19).

year.title: Palm Sunday
how: Read Mark 11:1–11 aloud.
Bring home a palm cross from church, or make one from a strip of paper.
Keep it somewhere visible until Easter.
year.why: Crowds waved branches as Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a donkey, a king who came in peace (Zechariah 9:9).

year.title: A supper on Maundy Thursday
how: Eat a simple meal with bread and a cup.
Read John 13:1–15, Jesus washing his friends' feet.
If you are brave, wash one another's hands.
year.why: 'Maundy' comes from the Latin mandatum, 'commandment': 'A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another' (John 13:34).

year.title: Good Friday
how: Keep the day quiet: no music, simple food.
Read the Passion, Mark 15, in one sitting.
At three in the afternoon, the hour Jesus died, stop for a minute's silence.
year.why: Christians have kept this day with fasting and silence since the earliest centuries. In Britain hot cross buns, marked with the cross, are its food.

year.title: Easter morning
how: Greet each other with the ancient words: 'Christ is risen!' and the reply, 'He is risen indeed!'
Read John 20:1–18 at breakfast.
Hide eggs, or give them: new life breaking out of a shell.
year.why: This is the oldest and greatest feast of the Church. The greeting is still used every Easter, especially by the Orthodox.

year.title: Pentecost
how: Wear or put out something red.
Read Acts 2:1–13.
Pray for someone you know who speaks another language, or comes from another country.
year.why: The Spirit came on the first Christians like wind and fire, and each heard the good news in their own language. Many call it the Church's birthday.

year.title: Harvest thanksgiving
how: Give a bag of food to a food bank.
Name everyone and everything that brought tonight's meal to the table.
Sing or say a grace of thanks.
year.why: 'While the earth remains, seed time and harvest... will not cease' (Genesis 8:22). Thanks is the first prayer.

year.title: Remembering the dead
year.when: All Saints and All Souls, 1–2 November
how: Light a candle for each person you have lost, and say their names.
Tell one story about each.
If you can, visit a grave and leave flowers.
year.why: Christians believe the dead are still held by God and that we are one family with them, 'the communion of saints' in the Creed.

start.title: Where to start, with children or without
start.line: You do not need to know much. Begin with three small things, in this order, and add the next only when the last has stuck.

steps.title: Say grace at one meal a day
steps.how: Use the short one in By heart: 'Come, Lord Jesus, be our guest'. Children can say it within a week.

steps.title: A Bible story at bedtime
steps.how: Tonight's story, then the three 'I wonder' questions and a one-line prayer. Ten minutes.

steps.title: One line by heart each week
steps.how: This week's words, read at breakfast every day. By Sunday, see who can say it. Children usually win.

start.couple: With a husband or wife: read today's story together at breakfast, and end the day with the night prayer in By heart. Two minutes each, side by side.

items.name: Martin Luther
items.what: wrote his Small Catechism (1529) for the head of each household to teach the family at home: the commandments, the creed, the Lord's Prayer, and short prayers for morning, evening and meals.

items.name: Thomas More
items.what: had Scripture read aloud at meals in his house at Chelsea, and talked it over with his children, whom he educated as seriously as any scholar's sons, daughters included.

items.name: Susanna Wesley
items.what: mother of John and Charles Wesley and of many other children, set aside time alone with each child every week to talk about their soul and their life.

items.name: Johann Sebastian Bach
items.what: made music at home with his large family; the household songbooks he kept for his wife Anna Magdalena include hymns and prayers alongside dances.

rule.line: A rule of life is a handful of practices you keep, freely, to give your life a shape. Monks wrote rules; so did Wesley's first Methodists. Choose one or two to begin.

items.title: Rest
items.line: One day a week, stop.
items.history: The Sabbath, from the Ten Commandments, was a gift to slaves and a protest against endless work. Christians kept Sunday, the day of the resurrection, as their day of rest and worship.
items.objection: Modern life doesn't stop; a day off can feel like a luxury or a burden.
items.start: Choose one thing you will not do this Sunday (work email, shopping) and one thing you will do for joy.

items.title: Fasting
items.line: Go without, to make room for God.
items.history: Jesus fasted forty days and assumed his followers would fast ('when you fast', Matthew 6:16). The early Church fasted on Wednesdays and Fridays; Lent grew from the fast before Easter.
items.objection: It can become dieting, or pride, or harm. Anyone with a health condition or a history of eating problems should fast from something other than food.
items.start: Give up one thing for one day this week (a meal, coffee, your phone in the evening) and use the time to pray or give.

items.title: Giving
items.line: Hold money with an open hand.
items.history: The Old Testament tithe was a tenth of the harvest. The first Christians shared so that 'there was no one among them who lacked' (Acts 4:34). John Wesley's rule: gain all you can, save all you can, give all you can.
items.objection: Giving can be guilt-driven, or used to buy a clear conscience instead of changing how we live.
items.start: Choose a percentage you will give this month, and decide where it goes.

items.title: The examen
items.line: Look back on each day with God.
items.history: Ignatius of Loyola (1491–1556) taught his followers never to skip it: a few minutes each evening to notice where God was, give thanks, and own your failures. Rose Window's evening moment is built on it.
items.objection: Looking back can turn into anxious self-scrutiny.
items.start: Tonight, ask two questions: what am I most grateful for today, and what do I wish I had done differently?

items.title: Slow reading
items.line: Read a few verses as if they were written to you.
items.history: Lectio divina, 'holy reading', comes from the monasteries: read, meditate, pray, rest. The Carthusian Guigo II wrote it down as a ladder in the twelfth century.
items.objection: It can make a text mean whatever you feel. It works best alongside study of what the text meant.
items.start: Take tomorrow's story. Read it three times, slowly. Notice one word that catches you, and talk to God about it.

items.title: Hospitality
items.line: Make room at your table.
items.history: The first Christians were known for welcoming strangers, the sick and the poor; even the emperor Julian, who hated them, complained that they cared for pagan poor as well as their own.
items.objection: Homes are small and lives are busy; hospitality can feel like performance.
items.start: Invite one person this month who might be alone. Keep the food simple.

items.title: Pilgrimage
items.line: Make a journey on purpose.
items.history: Christians have walked to Jerusalem, Rome, Canterbury and Santiago for 1,600 years. The journey itself is the prayer.
items.objection: It can become tourism, or a way of buying merit.
items.start: Walk to a church or holy place near you, alone or with one other, and spend ten minutes in silence when you arrive.

rhythm.title: Your rhythm
rhythm.line: A rule starts with a rhythm. Here is the one Rose Window is built around; keep what helps.

items.how: Before your phone, or with your first coffee. Read, look, take one question into the day.
At lunch, on the train, or after the children are in bed. Walk the halls of Explore in order.
Read it each morning; say it from memory by Sunday.
Alone or with your family: the Lord's Prayer, or the short prayers in By heart.
One of the great works: Evensong, a painting, a cathedral.

words.title: Words of the great
words.line: Fifteen sentences that made the West, from Moses to Lincoln. Each is short enough to carry. Start with the first, and add one a week.

items.line: Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one.
items.why: The Shema, said by Jews morning and evening for nearly three thousand years: the first words of Western faith.

items.when: a prophet of Judah, about 700 BC
items.line: to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?
items.why: The whole of religion in one sentence.

items.when: at his trial in Athens, 399 BC
items.line: the unexamined life is not worth living
items.why: Said by a man on trial for his life, who would not stop asking questions.

items.line: by doing just actions we come to be just
items.why: Character is built by practice: the idea behind every habit in this app.

items.when: the Sermon on the Plain, about AD 30
items.line: As you would like people to do to you, do exactly so to them.
items.why: The golden rule. If you remember only one sentence, remember this.

items.when: a letter to Corinth, about AD 55
items.line: Love is patient and is kind.
items.why: Read at more weddings than any other passage.

items.when: Roman emperor, on campaign, about AD 170
items.line: Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years.
items.why: The most powerful man in the world, writing notes to himself about death and goodness.

items.line: Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee.
items.why: The first sentence of the first autobiography, and the best description of human longing.

items.line: all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well.
items.why: Written in a plague century by a woman who had nearly died: hope that is not naive.

items.line: Midway upon the journey of our life I found myself within a forest dark
items.why: The opening of the greatest Christian poem: everyone gets lost, and the way out begins there.

items.line: What a piece of work is man
items.why: Human greatness and human dust in one speech.

items.line: No man is an island, entire of itself
items.why: Written on what he thought was his deathbed, hearing a funeral bell.

items.line: They also serve who only stand and wait.
items.why: For anyone who cannot do what they once could.

items.line: Let nothing disturb thee
items.why: Kept in her prayer book: a pocket prayer for anxious days.

items.line: With malice toward none, with charity for all
items.why: How to end a war: Lincoln, who knew the Bible by heart, speaking as it taught him.

great.title: The great works
great.line: The music, art and places that people have travelled to for centuries, because they make the faith visible and audible. Hear one, see one, go to one. Each is worth a journey once in your life; several are free.

hear.title: Choral Evensong
hear.where: Any cathedral or college chapel in England, most days, around 5 pm; free
hear.why: Sung prayer at dusk, unchanged in shape since 1549. You can sit at the back and say nothing.

hear.title: A Festival of Nine Lessons and Carols
hear.where: Christmas Eve, on the radio worldwide since 1928, or queue for a seat
hear.why: Nine Bible readings from the fall to the birth of Christ, with carols between.

hear.title: St Matthew Passion
hear.where: Performed across Europe in Holy Week; at its home, the Thomaskirche in Leipzig, most years
hear.why: The story of Jesus's death in three hours of music; many think it the greatest work ever written.

hear.title: Messiah
hear.where: Advent and Christmas, everywhere; look for a 'scratch' performance where the audience sings
hear.why: The whole Christian story in Scripture's own words. Audiences still stand for the Hallelujah chorus.

hear.title: Mass in B minor
hear.where: Concert halls and churches, any season
hear.why: Bach's summary of everything he knew, set to the ancient words of the Mass.

hear.title: Gregorian chant at a monastery
hear.where: Vespers in the evening at an abbey such as Solesmes in France or Maria Laach in Germany; visitors welcome
hear.why: The oldest music of the West, still sung where it was born: in monasteries, every day.

see.title: The Baptism of Christ
see.why: Stillness and light: one of the calmest paintings in the world, and an easy first visit.

see.title: The Sistine Chapel
see.where: Vatican Museums, Rome; book ahead, go early
see.why: Creation on the ceiling, the Last Judgement on the wall: the Bible painted for the whole of Europe.

see.title: The Calling of Saint Matthew
see.where: San Luigi dei Francesi, Rome; free, in a working church
see.why: A beam of light, a pointing hand, and a tax collector who cannot believe he is chosen.

see.title: The Ghent Altarpiece
see.why: The Adoration of the Lamb: heaven as a meadow, painted with every leaf.

see.title: The Isenheim Altarpiece
see.why: Painted for a hospital: the most harrowing crucifixion in art, and a blazing resurrection.

see.title: The Last Supper
see.where: Santa Maria delle Grazie, Milan; book weeks ahead, fifteen minutes inside
see.why: The moment Jesus says one of you will betray me, and twelve men react.

see.title: The Scrovegni Chapel
see.why: The life of Christ round the walls of one small chapel, where Western painting learned to show feeling.

go.title: Your nearest cathedral
go.why: Go on an ordinary weekday. Walk slowly from the west door to the altar, as Explore's halls do, and sit for ten minutes.

go.title: Chartres Cathedral
go.why: The most complete medieval cathedral, with its 13th-century glass and the labyrinth on the floor.

go.title: Sainte-Chapelle
go.why: Built in the 1240s as a reliquary: walls made almost entirely of stained glass.

go.title: Hagia Sophia
go.why: Justinian's church of Holy Wisdom (537), the greatest building of the ancient world.

go.title: Assisi
go.why: The hill town of Francis and Clare, with Giotto's frescoes in the basilica.

go.title: Canterbury Cathedral
go.why: Where Thomas Becket was killed in 1170, and the goal of Chaucer's pilgrims.

go.title: Cologne Cathedral
go.why: Begun in 1248 and finished in 1880; the shrine of the Three Kings.

go.title: The Camino de Santiago
go.where: northern Spain, to Santiago de Compostela
go.why: The great pilgrim road of the Middle Ages, walked again by hundreds of thousands each year.

greats.title: Live like the greats
greats.line: Thirteen people who built the West on its faith and its learning. Spend seven days with one of them: what they knew by heart, how they lived, and one step a day for you.

people.name: Marcus Aurelius
people.who: Roman emperor and Stoic philosopher, who wrote his private notebook while at war on the Danube frontier.
knew: leaves-of-the-forest
Homer's lines on the generations of men, which he quotes from memory in the Meditations (X.34).
within-our-power
The teaching of Epictetus, whose Discourses he was given as a young man (Meditations I.7) and quotes again and again.
people.did: Each day he wrote short notes to himself in Greek, never meant for anyone else; we call them the Meditations. He began his mornings by preparing to meet difficult people without anger.
people.you: Each morning, write one line to yourself about how you mean to treat people today.
people.understood: That we cannot control what happens to us, only how we respond; and that the people who wrong us are our own kin.
people.hook: The most powerful man in the world, writing notes to himself to stay good.
story: Marcus was born in Rome to a rich family. The emperor Hadrian noticed the boy and arranged for him to be adopted into the imperial line. He had the best teachers in the empire, and in the first book of the Meditations he thanks each of them by name: one for teaching him to bear pain, another, Junius Rusticus, for lending him his own copy of the teachings of Epictetus.

He became emperor at forty and at once insisted on sharing power with his adoptive brother. His reign was one disaster after another: a plague brought back by the army from the East that killed millions, floods, famine, and invasions across the Danube. He sold palace treasures at auction rather than raise taxes to pay for the war.

In his fifties, often ill, he spent years in army camps on the northern frontier. There, at night, he wrote in Greek a notebook to himself. Two of its books end with a note of where he was: 'among the Quadi, on the Gran', and 'at Carnuntum'. He died on campaign in 180. The notebook survived by chance, and we call it the Meditations.
day: When he did not want to get up, he told himself that he was rising to do the work of a human being, for which he was made (Meditations V.1).
He prepared to meet the meddling, the ungrateful and the arrogant, and reminded himself that they were his kin and could not harm him (II.1).
The work of an emperor: hearing cases and petitions, often far into the night, and commanding an army in the field.

people.name: Elizabeth I
people.who: Queen of England for forty-five years, the age of Shakespeare, who saw off the Spanish Armada and settled the Church of England.

In 1593, aged sixty, she translated Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy from Latin herself, in about a month.
people.did: As a girl she studied Greek and Latin every day with her tutor Roger Ascham, who boasted of how much she read; as queen she still translated for pleasure, and prayed in her private chapel daily. Her motto was Video et taceo, 'I see and say nothing'.

people.understood: That a ruler must hold steady under threat and keep her own counsel; and that the old books, Boethius above all, teach how to bear a fortune that turns.
people.hook: A princess who survived prison by learning, and ruled for forty-five years.
story: Her mother, Anne Boleyn, was executed when Elizabeth was two. She grew up in the schoolroom. At eleven she translated a French book of devotion into English as a New Year's gift for her stepmother, Catherine Parr. Her tutor Roger Ascham boasted that she read more Greek in a day than some clergy read Latin in a week.

After a rebellion against her sister, Queen Mary, Elizabeth was sent to the Tower of London, certain she would die. Nothing was proved against her, and she was moved to house arrest at Woodstock. She learned there what she later lived by: to see everything and say little.

As queen she faced the Spanish Armada and rode out to her army at Tilbury. Five years later, at sixty, grieved by news from France, she translated the whole of Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy from Latin in about a month, the book Christians had read for a thousand years about bearing a fortune that turns.

Private prayers in her closet, many of which she wrote herself, in English, Latin, French, Italian and Greek.
Business of state, letters and audiences; and, for pleasure, music at the virginals and translation.

people.name: Johann Sebastian Bach
people.who: Organist and cantor in Leipzig, thought by many the greatest composer who ever lived.

Paul Gerhardt's hymn, which he set five times in the St Matthew Passion.

people.understood: That all work, done well, can be offered to God. In the margin of his Bible he wrote that where there is devotional music, God is always present with his grace.

story: Bach came from a family of musicians. By ten he had lost both parents and went to live with his elder brother. His early biography tells how the boy copied out a book of keyboard music his brother had forbidden him, by moonlight, over six months, only to have it taken away.

As a young organist he took four weeks' leave and walked some four hundred kilometres north to Lübeck to hear the great Buxtehude play. He stayed nearly four months. His church council reprimanded him. He did not regret it.

As cantor of St Thomas's in Leipzig he ran the music of the city's main churches and taught at the school. In his first years he wrote a new cantata for nearly every Sunday. On Good Friday 1727 the St Matthew Passion was first heard. In his last year, nearly blind, he was still at work.

Teaching and rehearsing at the Thomasschule, where the family lived.

people.name: William Wilberforce
people.who: The Member of Parliament who led the twenty-year campaign that abolished the British slave trade in 1807.
knew: His sons record that he learned the whole of Psalm 119, all 176 verses, by heart on his walks from Hyde Park Corner to the House of Commons.
people.did: He kept the first part of each day for prayer and Scripture before the business of Parliament, and kept Sunday free of politics altogether.
people.you: Keep the first half hour of your day for prayer and reading, before any news or messages.
people.understood: That patient, unglamorous work over a lifetime can end a great evil. The bill to abolish slavery itself passed the Commons three days before he died.
people.hook: A rich young MP who nearly gave up politics for God, then spent his life ending the slave trade.
story: Wilberforce was elected to Parliament at twenty-one: rich, witty, a gambler and a famous singer at parties. On a tour of Europe he read the New Testament in Greek with a friend and was converted. He thought he should leave politics. The old clergyman John Newton, once a slave-ship captain, told him God might use him where he was.

Encouraged by his friend William Pitt, he took up the cause of abolition. On 28 October 1787 he wrote in his journal that God had set before him two great objects: the end of the slave trade, and the reform of the nation's manners.

Year after year his bill failed. In February 1807 the Commons voted to abolish the trade by 283 to 16, and members rose to cheer him while he sat with his head in his hands. The Act to end slavery itself passed in July 1833. He heard of it three days before he died.
day: Prayer and Scripture before any business: he wrote in his journal that he must keep this time, and grieved when he lost it.
He is said to have recited Psalm 119, the longest psalm, which he knew by heart.
Parliament, letters, committees and friends, often till late.
No politics at all: church, family and rest.

people.name: Abraham Lincoln

people.understood: That a nation can be judged by a justice higher than its own. His Second Inaugural reads the war through the Psalms and the Gospels, and ends with 'malice toward none'.
people.hook: Less than a year of school, and the English of the King James Bible and Shakespeare.
story: Lincoln was born in a log cabin in Kentucky. He wrote that his schooling came 'by littles' and did not add up to a year. His stepmother brought books into the house, and he read the Bible, Aesop, The Pilgrim's Progress and a life of Washington until he knew them, walking miles to borrow more.

Accepting his party's nomination for the Senate, he took his text from Jesus: 'A house divided against itself cannot stand.' The nation could not stay half slave and half free. He lost the election, but the speech and the debates that followed made him known across the country.

In March 1865, with the war nearly won, he gave his second inaugural address: a short sermon, quoting the Bible, on a nation under judgement. It ends 'With malice toward none, with charity for all'. Six weeks later he was shot.

people.name: Frederick Douglass
people.who: Born into slavery in Maryland, he taught himself to read, escaped, and became the most powerful voice for abolition in America.
knew: psalm-137-1

people.understood: That learning to read is the road to freedom. When his master forbade his lessons, he saw that knowledge was exactly what slavery feared.
people.hook: He taught himself to read in secret, and became the greatest speaker in America.
story: As an enslaved boy sent to Baltimore, Douglass was taught the alphabet by the woman of the house, until her husband stopped her: learning, he said, would make the boy unfit to be a slave. Douglass wrote that at that moment he understood the pathway from slavery to freedom. He traded bread with white boys in the street for reading lessons.

At twenty he escaped, by train and steamboat to New York, dressed as a sailor and carrying a free sailor's papers. Three years later, at an anti-slavery meeting in Nantucket, he stood up and spoke, and was hired at once as a lecturer.

His Narrative of 1845 made him famous and put him in danger, so he spent two years speaking in Britain and Ireland, where friends bought his legal freedom. Back in Rochester he started his own newspaper, and in 1852 gave the speech 'What to the slave is the Fourth of July?'.

A secret Sunday school for other enslaved men, teaching them to read.

story: She was born Araminta Ross, enslaved in Maryland. As a teenager she was struck on the head by a heavy weight thrown by an overseer at someone else. For the rest of her life she had seizures and vivid dreams, which she took to be from God.
Fearing she would be sold, she escaped alone, walking about ninety miles to Philadelphia. She said later that when she crossed into freedom she looked at her hands to see if she was the same person.

She went back about thirteen times and led some seventy people to freedom, among them her parents and brothers, and said she never lost a passenger. People called her Moses. In the Civil War she guided a raid on the Combahee River that freed more than seven hundred.

people.name: Florence Nightingale
people.who: Founder of modern nursing, who cut deaths in the military hospitals of the Crimean War and changed public health with statistics.

people.hook: She heard a call at sixteen, defied her family, and made nursing a profession.
story: On 7 February 1837, aged sixteen, she wrote that God spoke to her and called her to his service. Her rich family expected her to marry. It took her sixteen years, and a refusal of a man she loved, before they let her train as a nurse.

In the Crimean War she took thirty-eight nurses to the army hospital at Scutari, where soldiers lay in filth. She walked the wards at night with a lamp, and the newspapers made her famous. After the war she used statistics, and a diagram of her own design, to show that most of the dead had died of disease, not wounds.

Ill for most of the rest of her long life, she worked from her bed: she founded the first school of nursing at St Thomas's in 1860, wrote Notes on Nursing, and pressed ministers for reform for fifty years.

Private notes and prayers; her copy of Thomas à Kempis's The Imitation of Christ is full of her markings.

people.hook: Bottom of the class, prize-winner in poetry, and the voice of a nation alone.
story: He was kept in the bottom form at Harrow for three years. But there he was drilled in plain English until, he said, he had the structure of the British sentence in his bones; and he won a prize open to the whole school by reciting twelve hundred lines of Macaulay without a mistake.

As a young war correspondent in South Africa he was captured by the Boers, escaped from prison in Pretoria, and made his way three hundred miles to freedom. He came home famous and was elected to Parliament the next year.

He became Prime Minister in May 1940 as France fell. His speeches that summer carried the rhythms of the Bible and the poets he knew by heart. In a broadcast in April 1941 he quoted Clough, 'westward, look, the land is bright'; in August he chose 'O God, our help in ages past' for a service at sea with Roosevelt.

story: Solzhenitsyn was an artillery captain at the front when he was arrested for criticising Stalin in letters to a friend. He was sentenced to eight years in the labour camps.

people.who: Leader of the struggle against apartheid, imprisoned for twenty-seven years, then the first President of a free South Africa.
knew: henley-invictus
Kept in the heads of the prisoners on Robben Island; he recited it to the men around him.
julius-caesar-cowards
The lines he marked and signed in the prisoners' secret copy of Shakespeare, 16 December 1977.
people.did: In prison he exercised every morning in his cell, studied for a law degree by correspondence, and tended a small garden, which he said gave him a taste of freedom.
people.you: Tend one small thing every day, a plant, a skill or a friendship, however hard the day.
people.understood: That no one can take your inner freedom, and that forgiving his jailers freed him as much as them. Educated in Methodist schools, he never lost the language of the Bible.
people.hook: Twenty-seven years in prison, and he came out without bitterness.
story: At his trial for sabotage he spoke for three hours, ending that the ideal of a free and democratic society was one for which he was prepared to die. He was sentenced to life imprisonment, aged forty-five.

He broke stones in a lime quarry by day and slept on a mat in a tiny cell. The prisoners shared a copy of Shakespeare; Mandela marked in it the line from Julius Caesar, 'Cowards die many times before their deaths'. He studied law by correspondence and kept 'Invictus' in his head.
He was released in February 1990, after twenty-seven years. In 1994 he became South Africa's first president elected by all its people, and invited one of his former jailers to his inauguration.
day: Exercise in his cell: running on the spot, press-ups, sit-ups.
Hard labour in the quarry, and talk with the other prisoners, which they called the university.
Study for his degree, and letters, which were few and censored.
A small garden, which he said gave him a taste of freedom.
week: Learn the first verse of 'Invictus'.
Learn 'Cowards die many times before their deaths'.
Begin the day with one small act of discipline, before anything else.
Tend one small thing: a plant, a skill or a friendship.
Pray for someone who has wronged you.
Study something for twenty minutes.
Say 'Invictus' to someone.
read: Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (1994).
Nelson Mandela, Conversations with Myself (2010).
Ashwin Desai, Reading Revolution: Shakespeare on Robben Island (2012).
sources: Statement from the dock, Rivonia Trial, 20 April 1964.
Long Walk to Freedom (1994), parts 8–10.
The 'Robben Island Shakespeare' of Sonny Venkatrathnam, signed by Mandela on 16 December 1977.

remember.title: Worth remembering
remember.line: Each Sunday, one speech or poem that held someone up when it mattered: the story, the words, why it is worth having by heart, and how to say it.

items.title: The Gettysburg Address
items.hook: Two minutes, 272 words, and a nation told what it was for.
scene: Four months after the bloodiest battle of the American Civil War, the town of Gettysburg dedicated a cemetery for the Union dead. The main speaker, the orator Edward Everett, spoke for two hours. Lincoln, invited almost as an afterthought, spoke for about two minutes. The photographers were still setting up when he sat down.

He had written it in the White House and revised it to the last; five copies in his own hand survive. Newspapers divided on party lines: some called it silly, others saw at once what it was. Everett wrote to him the next day that he wished he had come as near the heart of the occasion in two hours as Lincoln had in two minutes.
why: Lincoln had almost no schooling, but he had the King James Bible and Shakespeare in his head, and you can hear both: 'Four score and seven years', 'consecrate', 'hallow', 'a new birth of freedom'. He takes a battlefield and turns it into a promise: that the dead shall not have died in vain. Learn it and you will have, in under three hundred words, the case for why free people must keep choosing freedom.
say: Slow down on the three verbs: 'we can not dedicate, we can not consecrate, we can not hallow'.
The last sentence is one long climb; take a breath before 'that this nation, under God'.
Lean on 'of', 'by' and 'for' in the final line, not on 'people'.
sources: Garry Wills, Lincoln at Gettysburg (1992).
Edward Everett to Lincoln, 20 November 1863 (Library of Congress).

items.title: Love bade me welcome
items.hook: A seventeenth-century country parson's poem, and the young philosopher who found Christ while saying it.
scene: George Herbert was a brilliant Cambridge orator who gave up a career at court to become the parson of a tiny parish near Salisbury. He died at thirty-nine in 1633, and sent his poems to a friend to publish or burn. 'Love (III)' is the last poem in the book.

Three centuries later, in 1938, the French philosopher Simone Weil, a Jewish-born agnostic, spent Holy Week at the abbey of Solesmes, suffering violent headaches. A young Englishman there showed her Herbert's poems. She learned 'Love' by heart and recited it to herself through the pain, as a discipline of attention. She later wrote to a priest that while she was saying it, Christ himself came down and took possession of her.
why: It is a whole theology in eighteen lines: a guest who feels unworthy, a host who will not let him go, and a meal. Every excuse the soul makes, Love answers. It is the poem to learn if you think you are too far gone to be welcome.
say: It is a conversation: give Love and the soul different voices.
Pause after 'Who made the eyes but I?'
Say the last line simply, almost quietly: 'So I did sit and eat.'
sources: George Herbert, The Temple (1633).
Simone Weil, letter to Father Perrin, 15 May 1942 ('Spiritual Autobiography'), in Waiting for God.

items.title: In Flanders fields
items.hook: For Remembrance Sunday: a doctor's poem written beside a friend's grave, and the reason we wear poppies.
scene: John McCrae was a Canadian army doctor at the second battle of Ypres in 1915. On 2 May his friend Lieutenant Alexis Helmer was killed by a shell, and McCrae, in the absence of a chaplain, led the burial himself. Poppies were already growing between the graves. The next day, the story goes, he wrote this poem in twenty minutes, sitting on the back of an ambulance.

It was published in Punch that December and became the most famous poem of the war. An American teacher, Moina Michael, read it in 1918 and vowed always to wear a red poppy; from her the poppy spread across the English-speaking world. McCrae died of pneumonia in France in January 1918.
why: The dead speak, briefly, and ask the living one thing: do not break faith with us. It is fifteen lines, easy to learn, and on Remembrance Sunday you will hear it read in churches and at war memorials. Learn it so that you can say it with them, and so that you know what you are being asked.
say: Read it slowly, as the dead might speak: there is no hurry.
Let 'In Flanders fields' fall quietly at the end of each verse.
Give the torch lines a little more strength: it is a charge, not a lament.
sources: John McCrae, In Flanders Fields and Other Poems (1919).
Moina Michael, The Miracle Flower (1941).

items.title: The whole earth for their tomb
items.hook: The oldest great speech of the West: an Athenian leader honouring the first dead of a long war.
scene: At the end of the first year of the war between Athens and Sparta, the Athenians held a public funeral for their dead. The bones lay in cypress coffins, one for each tribe, with an empty bier for the missing. Pericles, the city's leading statesman, was chosen to speak.

The historian Thucydides wrote the speech down, in his own words but faithful, he said, to its sense. Pericles barely mentions the dead men by name. He praises the city they died for: a democracy, open to the world, where people love beauty without extravagance and wisdom without softness. A year later plague struck Athens, and Pericles himself died of it.
why: It is the first great statement of what a free city is, and it was read in British schools for centuries; Lincoln's Gettysburg Address follows its shape. These lines are the most beautiful: the real monument to the dead is not stone but the memory in living hearts.
say: Let 'the whole earth' be wide: pause before it.
Drop your voice on 'except that of the heart'.
Remember it is said at a graveside.
sources: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War II.34–46, tr. Richard Crawley (1874).

items.title: What to the slave is the Fourth of July?
items.hook: Invited to celebrate American freedom, an escaped slave told the audience the truth.
scene: The Rochester Ladies' Anti-Slavery Society invited Frederick Douglass to speak for Independence Day. He chose the fifth, not the fourth, and began by praising the founders and the Declaration of Independence. Then he turned. 'This Fourth of July is yours, not mine.'

Douglass had escaped slavery in Maryland fourteen years earlier. He had taught himself to read and become the most powerful speaker in America. Midway through the speech he quoted Psalm 137, the song of the exiles by the rivers of Babylon, and asked how slaves could sing in a strange land. He ended in hope, quoting Isaiah: the arm of the Lord is not shortened.
why: It shows what great speaking can do: hold up a nation's own ideals to it and ask whether it means them. It is not anti-American; Douglass called the Constitution a 'glorious liberty document'. It is a prophet's speech, in the line of Amos. Learn these lines and you will understand why justice must be named before it can be done.
say: The first two lines are a hinge: let a silence fall after 'You may rejoice, I must mourn.'
Ask the question as a real question, to the room.
Do not shout the answer; its force is in its precision.
sources: Frederick Douglass, My Bondage and My Freedom (1855), appendix (Gutenberg #202).
David W. Blight, Frederick Douglass: Prophet of Freedom (2018).

items.title: To an unknown god
items.hook: Where Jerusalem first spoke to Athens: a Jewish teacher on the hill of the philosophers.
scene: On his travels through Greece Paul came to Athens, still the university city of the ancient world. He argued in the market place with Epicurean and Stoic philosophers, who took him to the Areopagus, the rock where the city's council met, to explain himself.

He did not begin with the Hebrew Scriptures, which they did not know. He began with an altar he had seen 'to an unknown god', and quoted their own poets: Epimenides and Aratus. Some mocked when he spoke of resurrection; a few believed, among them a council member, Dionysius, and a woman named Damaris.
why: It is the model of speaking to people who do not share your beliefs: start where they are, honour what is true in their tradition, then say what is new. 'In him we live, move, and have our being' is one of the great sentences of the Bible. It is a fitting first Sunday of Advent: God is not far from each one of us.
say: Begin warmly, not as an accusation: 'very religious' is a compliment.
Point, as Paul did, on 'this inscription'.
Let the last line be quiet and close: it is about nearness.
sources: Epimenides (via Titus 1:12) and Aratus, Phaenomena 5.

items.title: Horatius at the bridge
items.who: Thomas Babington Macaulay, and Winston Churchill
items.hook: The poem a struggling schoolboy learned by heart, and carried into 1940.
scene: At Harrow Winston Churchill was near the bottom of the school, held back in the lowest form for three years. But he won a prize open to the whole school by reciting twelve hundred lines of Macaulay's Lays of Ancient Rome without a mistake. He tells the story in My Early Life (1930).

The Lays retell legends of early Rome. In 'Horatius', the city is about to fall to an invading army; one soldier, Horatius, offers to hold the narrow bridge with two companions while the Romans cut it down behind them. Churchill knew it all his life, and in the summer of 1940, when Britain stood alone, his speeches carried the same music.
why: It is the poem of standing your ground when everything is against you. Generations of schoolchildren learned it, and it shaped the courage of men who led their countries through war. Eight lines is enough to start: the question it asks, 'how can man die better', is one every person faces.
say: It is a ballad: let the rhythm carry you, tum-ti-tum.
Make 'brave Horatius' a name you admire.
Slow down on 'For the ashes of his fathers'.
sources: Thomas Babington Macaulay, Lays of Ancient Rome (1842).
Winston S. Churchill, My Early Life (1930), chapter 2.

items.title: The heart and stomach of a king
items.hook: A queen rides out to her army as the Armada threatens invasion.
scene: In the summer of 1588 the Spanish Armada sailed up the Channel to carry an invasion army from the Netherlands to England. The queen's army gathered at Tilbury, on the Thames, to defend London. Against her council's advice, Elizabeth, fifty-four, rode out among them.

Her words were written down by Leonel Sharp, a chaplain who was there; his version was published decades later. By then the Armada had already been scattered by English fire ships and storms, though no one at Tilbury yet knew it.
why: She turns a weakness into strength in one sentence, with complete self-command. It is the best example in English of a leader standing in front of frightened people and taking the fear on herself. Learn the three lines; they will do for any day you feel outmatched.
say: Do not apologise in the first line; state it plainly.
Pause before 'but'.
Let 'and of a king of England too' land with a smile.
sources: Leonel Sharp, letter to the Duke of Buckingham (published 1654).
Janet M. Green, 'I Myself: Queen Elizabeth I's Oration at Tilbury Camp', Sixteenth Century Journal 28 (1997).

items.title: Abide with me
items.who: Henry Francis Lyte, and Edith Cavell
items.hook: A dying vicar's hymn, sung by a nurse in her cell the night before her execution.
scene: Henry Francis Lyte was the vicar of a fishing town in Devon. In 1847, dying of tuberculosis, he preached his last sermon and gave his family this hymn. He died in Nice a few weeks later.

In 1915 Edith Cavell, an English nurse running a training school in occupied Brussels, was condemned by a German court for helping some two hundred Allied soldiers escape. On the night before her execution the Anglican chaplain, Stirling Gahan, visited her cell. They received communion together and, at the end, said 'Abide with me' quietly together. She told him that patriotism was not enough; she must have no hatred or bitterness towards anyone.
why: It is the hymn for the end of a day and the end of a life: sung at funerals, at the Cup Final since 1927, at Remembrance. Its first verse is four lines that anyone can carry into a hospital room or a sleepless night.
say: It is a prayer: say it to someone, not to a room.
Let 'the darkness deepens' slow you down.
End on 'abide with me' as a request, not a statement.
sources: Henry Francis Lyte, Remains (1850).
H. Stirling T. Gahan's account of Edith Cavell's last night (1915), in A. A. Hoehling, A Whisper of Eternity (1957).

items.title: Invictus
items.who: William Ernest Henley, and Nelson Mandela
items.hook: A poem written in a hospital bed, kept alive in a prison cell.
scene: William Ernest Henley had tuberculosis of the bone; his left leg was amputated below the knee when he was a teenager. In 1873 doctors said the other leg must go too. He travelled to Edinburgh to be treated by the surgeon Joseph Lister, spent nearly two years in the infirmary, and saved the leg. There he wrote the poem later called 'Invictus', Latin for 'unconquered'.

On Robben Island, where Nelson Mandela spent eighteen of his twenty-seven years in prison, the prisoners passed poems and plays between them. Mandela kept 'Invictus' in his head and recited it to the men around him.
why: It is a poem of courage, not of faith; Henley thanks 'whatever gods may be', and a Christian would say the captain of the soul is God. But it is the best poem in English for holding your head up under blows you did not choose, and it held up a man who later forgave his jailers.
say: Keep it level and quiet: defiance does not need volume.
Let 'bloody, but unbowed' have its two halves.
The last two lines are short words: say each one.
sources: W. E. Henley, A Book of Verses (1888).
Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (1994).

items.title: If—
items.hook: For the new year: a father's advice in one long sentence.
scene: Kipling published 'If—' in 1910 in Rewards and Fairies, a book of stories for children. He said later that it was drawn from the character of Leander Starr Jameson, a doctor and adventurer he admired. Five years later his only son John was killed at the battle of Loos.

It became the most popular poem in Britain: in a BBC poll in 1995 it was voted the nation's favourite. Two of its lines are written above the players' entrance to the Centre Court at Wimbledon: 'If you can meet with Triumph and Disaster / And treat those two impostors just the same'.
why: It is a portrait of character: steadiness, honesty, patience, humility, endurance, all in one sentence that does not stop until the last line. Many find it too stoic; it does not mention God. But it describes what most of the greats in this app had, and it is a superb first poem to learn.
say: It is one sentence: keep it moving, and save your breath for the last two lines.
Give each 'If' a fresh start.
The ending is a blessing, not a boast.
sources: Rudyard Kipling, Rewards and Fairies (1910); Something of Myself (1937).

items.title: Give me liberty
items.hook: In a church, a lawyer argues that the time for petitions is over.
scene: The Second Virginia Convention met in St John's Church in Richmond because it was the only building large enough. The delegates were debating whether to raise a militia against Britain. Patrick Henry, a country lawyer famous for his speaking, rose to say that the war had in effect already begun.

No text was written down at the time. Henry's biographer William Wirt reconstructed the speech in 1817 from the memories of men who heard it; historians debate how much is Henry and how much Wirt. Within a month, the first shots of the American Revolution were fired at Lexington.
why: Whatever its exact words, it is the classic of the deliberative speech: the moment of decision, put as a choice between two things. It is also a warning: words this strong are only honest if the speaker is willing to pay the price they name.
say: Build the two questions; then let 'Forbid it, Almighty God!' break out.
Pause before 'but as for me'.
Say the last words as a vow, not a slogan.
sources: William Wirt, Sketches of the Life and Character of Patrick Henry (1817).
Thomas S. Kidd, Patrick Henry: First Among Patriots (2011).

items.title: I would never rest
items.hook: A young MP spends three and a half hours making the case against the slave trade.
scene: Wilberforce was twenty-nine, a rich and popular MP who had experienced an evangelical conversion four years earlier and wondered whether to leave politics. John Newton, the former slave-ship captain turned clergyman, told him to stay. In May 1789 he moved his first resolutions against the slave trade in a speech of three and a half hours.

He did not attack the merchants; he said they were all guilty, himself included, for allowing it. The resolutions were delayed. He brought the motion again and again for eighteen years until the trade was abolished in 1807, and slavery itself was abolished in the British Empire three days before he died in 1833.
why: These lines are the moment a man decides his life's work. It is the speech to learn when you know something is wrong and need the resolve to keep at it.
say: The first sentence is a list of three: let each word land.
Slow down on 'let the consequences be what they would'.
The last line is a promise to yourself: say it as one.
sources: The Parliamentary History of England, vol. 28 (1816), 12 May 1789.
Eric Metaxas, Amazing Grace (2007); William Hague, William Wilberforce (2007).

items.title: The man in the arena
items.hook: A former president, in the oldest university in Paris, defends the people who try.
scene: A year after leaving the White House, Theodore Roosevelt toured Europe. At the Sorbonne he gave a long lecture called 'Citizenship in a Republic' to an audience of some two thousand, about what a republic needs from its citizens.
Most of it is forgotten. One paragraph is not: it has been quoted by presidents, athletes and businessmen ever since, and pinned above countless desks.
why: It answers the voice in every head that says don't try, you'll fail, people will laugh. Its moral is close to the parable of the talents: better to risk and fail than to bury what you were given.
say: It is one long sentence after the first: ride the 'who' clauses.
Hit 'dust and sweat and blood' with the consonants.
Slow right down on 'cold and timid souls'.
sources: Theodore Roosevelt, 'Citizenship in a Republic' (1910).

items.title: To strive, to seek, to find
items.hook: A grieving young poet imagines an old king setting sail one last time.
scene: In 1833 Tennyson's closest friend, Arthur Hallam, died suddenly in Vienna at twenty-two. Tennyson wrote 'Ulysses' within weeks; he said it expressed his feeling about 'the need of going forward and braving the struggle of life'. Years of grief later produced In Memoriam.

The hero is Homer's Odysseus, home at last, now old, who calls his ageing crew to sail out again beyond the sunset. Its last line was written on a wall in the athletes' village at the London Olympics in 2012.
why: It is the poem for anyone who feels their best days are behind them. 'Tho' much is taken, much abides' is a sentence worth carrying through any loss.
say: Begin as an invitation: 'Come, my friends'.
Let the long sentences roll like oars.
Give the last line four equal strokes.
sources: Alfred Tennyson, Poems (1842); Hallam Tennyson, Alfred Lord Tennyson: A Memoir (1897).

items.title: I to die, and you to live
items.hook: Condemned to death, a philosopher thanks his judges and walks out.
scene: At seventy, Socrates was tried before a jury of five hundred Athenians for corrupting the young and not believing in the city's gods. He refused to beg, and was condemned to death by drinking hemlock. Plato, his student, wrote down his defence, the Apology.

At the end, Socrates speaks to the jurors who voted to acquit him. Death, he says, is either a dreamless sleep or a journey to meet the great dead; neither is to be feared, and no evil can happen to a good man.
why: It is the West's first great speech in the face of death, and it shows how a person of conscience can stand unafraid. Christians read it for centuries alongside the deaths of the martyrs.
say: Say it calmly; Socrates is the only person in the room not afraid.
Pause before 'I to die, and you to live'.
End lightly on 'God only knows'.
sources: Plato, Apology 40c–42a, tr. Benjamin Jowett (1871).
